en.title: GPT Image 2.6 is here with one-sentence GIF generation — I'm more interested in whether it's fixed the noise issue.
en.summary: GPT Image 2.6 is officially live, adding transparent-background GIF and SVG vector graphics support, boosting generation speed by roughly 50%, and offering adjustable thinking levels through the API. Xiaowei ran real-world tests across multiple scenarios — e-commerce product shots, comic storyboards, and home interior layouts all proved workable, and noise issues improved slightly. But shortcomings remain: deformed fingers, garbled text in Chinese infographics, degrading quality after repeated iterative edits, and an increasingly plastic look. Check out how it actually performs.

en.title: How should multiple Agents share context? The key isn't syncing chat logs
en.summary: When multiple Agents work together, the handoff is where things break down: a model runs out of quota, the task changes hands, and the incoming Agent either drowns in the full chat history or has to feel its way from scratch. Title: Xcode MCP 助力运行时二进制分析
Published Time: 2026-11-05T02:36:12+00:00
iOS 客户端最头疼的一类 Crash：栈里全是系统库，无现成源码可参考。静态反汇编工具多数时候只能推导不能证实，且丢失运行时信息这样的关键线索，面对有些疑难杂症，运行时二进制分析在所难免。
而这样的分析需要环境构造、GUI 操作、业务复现等，AI 难以完全承担，更合理的是工程师与 AI 协同分析。

en.title: Xcode MCP enables runtime binary analysis
en.summary:
Xcode MCP powers runtime binary analysis

One of the most frustrating types of crash for iOS apps: the stack is full of system libraries, with no source code available for reference. Static disassembly tools can often only infer, not prove, and they lose key clues such as runtime information. For some tricky bugs, runtime binary analysis is unavoidable.

Such analysis requires environment setup, GUI operations, and reproducing app behavior, which AI cannot fully handle. A more reasonable approach is collaborative analysis between engineers and AI.

Although IDA can debug iOS, it is complex to operate, offers a poor experience, and lags in adaptation. lldb-mcp has no GUI and is better suited to automation. mcpbridge in newer Xcode provides an LLDB invocation channel, which appears to enable seamless collaboration.

EXC_BAD_ACCESS(SIGSEGV)
Trapped mach exception code 0x1, subcode 0x1d
0   libdispatch.dylib     dispatch_source_set_timer + 36
1   CFNetwork             URLConnectionLoader::loadWith
en.reason: An EXC_BAD_ACCESS crash with subcode 0x1d and a stack showing only dispatch_source_set_timer + 36 in libdispatch illustrates how Xcode's mcpbridge exposes LLDB to AI for setting breakpoints, reading registers and batch-verifying hypotheses, with engineers converging the results.

en.title: Without writing a single line of code: I built a 3D smart exhibition hall visualization dashboard with Codex
en.summary:
Without writing a single line of code: I built a 3D smart exhibition hall visualization wall with Codex

In earlier smart agriculture and smart highway projects, I had already run through the whole chain: research, design mockups, asset breakdown, modeling, and turning it all into a web page. This time, I moved the scenario to a corporate exhibition hall.

My first impression of indoor scenes was that the details have nowhere to hide. With a campus, you can start with building massing and road relationships; but once an exhibition hall camera moves in close, wall edges, glass thickness, monitor stands, display case seams and floor reflections all come into view. Putting a screen on a wall is easy — making it look like a real device that can actually play content and receive input means designing the model and the front end together.

This article follows the actual build chain: turn industry research into requirements, generate a complete design draft, break out assets and implementation boundaries, build the model with Blender-MCP, and finally wire it into the web page, the on-screen content and the camera tour. Rework along the way is covered in the relevant technical section, explaining why it changed and at which layer.

The project's business readouts use fixed sample data, and the model is a visualization-grade concept scene. The code here has been organized and trimmed from the actual project, with some context and error handling omitted; the parameters explain this particular implementation and should not be treated as a universal configuration for every exhibition hall.

## 1. Research the business first, then let Codex write out something executable…
en.reason: Codex was used to carry an article's full workflow from industry research and design drafts through Blender-MCP modeling to a Three.js web build, laying out six exhibition zones at 1920×1080 and grounding the demo with sample data of 120 visitors, 49 device records and 29 screens.

en.title: One Person Is an Entire Engineering Team: A 90-Day Monetization SOP for the Super Individual in the AI Era
en.summary:
One Person Is an Entire Engineering Team: The 90-Day Monetization SOP for Super-Individuals in the AI Era

You're sick of those headlines too. I want to talk about a smaller, harder, more verifiable goal: **complete one real transaction within 90 days.** Not "built a cool project," not "gained a bunch of followers"—someone willing to pay for what you deliver. Even if the first order is only 999 yuan.

Because going from 0 to 1 and from 1 to 100 are two entirely different skill sets. Most people get stuck at 0 to 1 not because their technical skills fall short, but because they've never closed the loop of "demand—delivery—payment."

For individual monetization, the biggest barrier used to be not technology but "trust" and "channels." You first had to prove you could do it, then prove you were reliable, and finally find someone willing to pay. Three mountains—climbing them alone is slow.

Lovable announced in September 2026 that its ARR reached $600 million, with a valuation of $13.3 billion. [1] The significance of this figure isn't how much money it makes, but that: **a large number of people who "shouldn't be building software" are starting to pay for "making a piece of software that works."**

Demand has been validated; what's left is supply. And the scarcest part of that supply
en.reason: A 90-day playbook for solo builders targets one real transaction, even a first order as low as 999 yuan, by closing the demand-delivery-payment loop and citing Lovable’s $600M ARR and $13.3B valuation as proof of demand.

> Who it's for: backend developers who know Spring Boot and want to get started with AI app development, but got scared off by a pile of new jargon.

## 1. A quick self-test: how many of these 5 questions can you answer?
1.   What do the "2 paths, 3 methods, 4 call types" of large model integration refer to?

If you can't answer 2 of the 5, this post is written for you.
I

en.title: Xcode MCP enables runtime binary analysis
en.summary:
Xcode MCP powers runtime binary analysis

One of the most frustrating types of crash for iOS apps: the stack is full of system libraries, with no source code available for reference. Static disassembly tools can often only infer, not prove, and they lose key clues such as runtime information. For some tricky bugs, runtime binary analysis is unavoidable.

Such analysis requires environment setup, GUI operations, and reproducing app behavior, which AI cannot fully handle. A more reasonable approach is collaborative analysis between engineers and AI.

Although IDA can debug iOS, it is complex to operate, offers a poor experience, and lags in adaptation. lldb-mcp has no GUI and is better suited to automation. mcpbridge in newer Xcode provides an LLDB invocation channel, which appears to enable seamless collaboration.

en.title: Without writing a single line of code: I built a 3D smart exhibition hall visualization dashboard with Codex
en.summary:
Without writing a single line of code: I built a 3D smart exhibition hall visualization wall with Codex

In earlier smart agriculture and smart highway projects, I had already run through the whole chain: research, design mockups, asset breakdown, modeling, and turning it all into a web page. This time, I moved the scenario to a corporate exhibition hall.

My first impression of indoor scenes was that the details have nowhere to hide. With a campus, you can start with building massing and road relationships; but once an exhibition hall camera moves in close, wall edges, glass thickness, monitor stands, display case seams and floor reflections all come into view. Putting a screen on a wall is easy — making it look like a real device that can actually play content and receive input means designing the model and the front end together.

This article follows the actual build chain: turn industry research into requirements, generate a complete design draft, break out assets and implementation boundaries, build the model with Blender-MCP, and finally wire it into the web page, the on-screen content and the camera tour. Rework along the way is covered in the relevant technical section, explaining why it changed and at which layer.

The project's business readouts use fixed sample data, and the model is a visualization-grade concept scene. The code here has been organized and trimmed from the actual project, with some context and error handling omitted; the parameters explain this particular implementation and should not be treated as a universal configuration for every exhibition hall.

en.title: One Person Is an Entire Engineering Team: A 90-Day Monetization SOP for the Super Individual in the AI Era
en.summary:
One Person Is an Entire Engineering Team: The 90-Day Monetization SOP for Super-Individuals in the AI Era

You're sick of those headlines too. I want to talk about a smaller, harder, more verifiable goal: **complete one real transaction within 90 days.** Not "built a cool project," not "gained a bunch of followers"—someone willing to pay for what you deliver. Even if the first order is only 999 yuan.

Because going from 0 to 1 and from 1 to 100 are two entirely different skill sets. Most people get stuck at 0 to 1 not because their technical skills fall short, but because they've never closed the loop of "demand—delivery—payment."

For individual monetization, the biggest barrier used to be not technology but "trust" and "channels." You first had to prove you could do it, then prove you were reliable, and finally find someone willing to pay. Three mountains—climbing them alone is slow.

Lovable announced in September 2026 that its ARR reached $600 million, with a valuation of $13.3 billion. [1] The significance of this figure isn't how much money it makes, but that: **a large number of people who "shouldn't be building software" are starting to pay for "making a piece of software that works."**

Demand has been validated; what's left is supply. And the scarcest part of that supply
en.reason: A 90-day playbook for solo builders targets one real transaction, even a first order as low as 999 yuan, by closing the demand-delivery-payment loop and citing Lovable’s $600M ARR and $13.3B valuation as proof of demand.

Backend to AI app development: I started by getting these 12 terms straight — one diagram to understand the architecture, RAG, Tool Calling, and MCP

Published Time: 2026-11-05T03:44:06+00:00

> Who it's for: backend developers who know Spring Boot and want to get started with AI app development, but got scared off by a pile of new jargon.
> What you'll walk away with: an architecture diagram you can memorize, a concept cheat sheet, a minimal piece of code that actually runs, and 5 pitfalls I've genuinely hit.
## 1. A quick self-test: how many of these 5 questions can you answer?
1.   What do the "2 paths, 3 methods, 4 call types" of large model integration refer to?
2.   What's the relationship between Bailian and Lingji DashScope? Which one should I use when writing code?
3.   In RAG, which of ETL and retrieval runs offline, and which runs on every request?
4.   What's the difference between Tool Calling and MCP? Why do we need the latter when we already have the former?
5.   When a model calls a tool, why do two rounds of Request/Response show up in the logs?
If you can't answer 2 of the 5, this post is written for you.
I
